assessment_summary: The statement is false. Two trees with the same degree sequence are not necessarily isomorphic. A simple counterexample can be found with two trees on 6 vertices, where both have the degree sequence (3, 2, 2, 1, 1, 1). In one tree, the degree 3 vertex is adjacent to two degree 2 vertices and one leaf. In the other, the degree 3 vertex is adjacent to one degree 2 vertex and two leaves. Because their structural neighborhoods differ, they cannot be isomorphic, yet their degree sequences match.
counterexample:
Consider two trees on the vertex set {1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6}:

Tree A has edges: {(1,2), (2,3), (3,4), (4,5), (3,6)}
Its degrees are:
deg(1) = 1
deg(2) = 2
deg(3) = 3
deg(4) = 2
deg(5) = 1
deg(6) = 1
Degree sequence of A: (3, 2, 2, 1, 1, 1)

Tree B has edges: {(1,2), (2,3), (3,4), (4,5), (2,6)}
Its degrees are:
deg(1) = 1
deg(2) = 3
deg(3) = 2
deg(4) = 2
deg(5) = 1
deg(6) = 1
Degree sequence of B: (3, 2, 2, 1, 1, 1)

Both graphs are connected and acyclic with 6 vertices and 5 edges, fulfilling the definition of a tree. They have identical degree sequences.

However, in Tree A, the only vertex of degree 3 (vertex 3) is adjacent to two vertices of degree 2 (vertices 2 and 4) and one vertex of degree 1 (vertex 6).
In Tree B, the only vertex of degree 3 (vertex 2) is adjacent to one vertex of degree 2 (vertex 3) and two vertices of degree 1 (vertices 1 and 6).

Since any isomorphism must map the unique vertex of degree 3 to the unique vertex of degree 3, and must preserve the degrees of adjacent vertices, there can be no edge-preserving bijection between their vertex sets. Thus, the two trees are not isomorphic despite having identical degree sequences.
